plan.contextChunk: This figure pairs two panels side by side to tie the circular and graphical pictures of the sine function together. At the left, drawn faintly in gray, is a unit circle crossed by its axes and by a fan of radii at the special angles. At the right is a Cartesian plot with a horizontal axis labeled x and a vertical axis labeled y ticked at 1, 0, and -1; a solid dark blue curve labeled y = sin(x) enters from the left with an arrowhead, passes through the origin, climbs to a peak of 1, and turns downward toward a second arrowhead. Four dashed orange vertical segments drop from the curve to x-axis ticks labeled pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, and pi/2, and four dashed teal horizontal lines run leftward from those same curve points, across the gap between panels, to matching heights on the gray circle. The teal connectors carry the comparison the figure is built for: the height of a point on the unit circle at a given angle is the value plotted above that angle on the graph. Reading the sine graph as a running record of height on the circle is what lets quadrant position account for the sign of the function.

interactionPlan.concept: The graph of the sine function is a continuous record of the vertical height (y-coordinate) of a point rotating around the unit circle.

interactions.label: Angle x
interactions.teaches: Moving the angle continuously updates the point on the circle and the graph simultaneously, showing that the sine graph's height is always exactly the circle point's y-coordinate.

interactions.label: Sweep quarter-turn
interactions.teaches: Tracing the first quarter-turn reveals how the rising height on the circle maps directly to the initial upward climb of the sine wave.

demo_steps.title: Mapping special angles
demo_steps.narration: The dashed teal lines show that at specific angles like pi/6, the vertical height on the unit circle perfectly matches the height of the sine curve.

demo_steps.title: A continuous record
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider to sweep the angle continuously. The sine curve is just a horizontal unrolling of the circle point's vertical position.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The sine graph translates the circular motion of a point into a left-to-right timeline of its vertical position.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Place the unit circle on the left and the Cartesian plot on the right. It is crucial that their horizontal axes (y=0) are perfectly collinear so the dashed teal lines are exactly horizontal. Use faint gray for the circle and radial grid to avoid clutter. Make the sine curve a bold, dark blue. The connecting lines (teal horizontal, orange vertical) should be dashed to read as guides rather than physical objects.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for angle x: the learner drags the angle on the unit circle, the matching point on y = sin(x) moves at the same time, and the horizontal height connector updates to show that sine is the circle point's y-coordinate.
- Animation for one quarter-turn sweep: the radius rotates from 0 to pi/2 while the sine graph is traced from the origin to its peak, making the graph read as a running record of vertical height on the circle.

authoredContext:
Notice how the sine values are positive between 0 and π, which correspond to the values of the sine function in quadrants I and II on the unit circle, and the sine values are negative between π and 2π, which correspond to the values of the sine function in quadrants III and IV on the unit circle. See the figure.

Plotting values of the sine function

A side-by-side graph of a unit circle and a graph of sin(x). The two graphs show the equivalence of the coordinates.
